opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to treat the lottery ticket hypothesis as a lens rather than a destination. When we wrote the original paper, the exciting part wasn't really "look, you can prune networks and they still train." People had known for decades that you could prune networks after training. The surprising part was that these sparse subnetworks existed early on and could train in isolation from a particular initialization. That says something about how optimization and initialization interact, and that's the question I'd love people to stay focused on.

So my advice to researchers is to resist a few temptations. One is to turn it into a leaderboard, finding a slightly better pruning heuristic or a slightly sparser ticket on CIFAR-10. That's fine as engineering, but it doesn't tell us much we didn't already know. Another is to assume that because tickets exist, there must be a cheap way to find them up front and save tons of compute. I'd love that to be true, but so far the evidence is pretty humbling. Finding tickets is expensive, and many methods that claim to find them at initialization don't hold up under careful sanity checks. We should be honest about that.

What I find more interesting are the scientific questions. Why do we need to rewind to a point slightly after initialization for larger networks rather than all the way back to step zero? What does that say about the early phase of training and the stability of optimization to noise like data ordering? What is the ticket actually capturing: the mask, the signs of the weights, the magnitudes, some interaction with the data? These are questions about how neural networks learn, and the lottery ticket setup gives us a handy experimental tool for poking at them.

I'd also encourage people to be rigorous and a little skeptical, including of my own work. Run the baselines. Check random pruning. Check whether results scale beyond small vision benchmarks. Some of the original findings didn't hold at scale without modification, and we only learned that by pushing on it. A research area stays healthy when people try to break its central claims, not just extend them.

So in short: treat it as a window into the science of deep learning, be careful about practical claims, and focus on the "why." That's where I think the real payoff is.

r001.rationale: The response encourages treating lottery tickets as a tool for studying deep learning and pursuing scientific questions; it does not advise abandoning the area.

r002.rationale: It applies lessons from the paper to research practice by urging researchers to focus on explanatory questions, test baselines, check scale, and challenge central claims.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing I'd say is: don't treat the lottery ticket hypothesis as a thing you need to prove or disprove. I think a lot of the follow-up work, including some of my own, got stuck in a mode of "does this trick work at scale, yes or no," and I'm not sure that's the most interesting question anymore. We already know the original rewind-to-initialization story doesn't hold cleanly for big networks. You have to rewind to an early point in training rather than iteration zero, and that's a genuinely different claim than the one in the paper title.

So what I'd push people toward is using lottery tickets as a lens rather than as a technique. The reason the result was interesting in the first place wasn't that you could make a small network. Pruning already did that. It was that a particular subnetwork, with a particular set of weights, was trainable in isolation, and a random reinitialization of the same structure wasn't. That tells you something about the loss landscape and about what happens in the first few hundred or few thousand steps of training. That's where I'd spend my time. What is it about those early iterations that makes the network stable? Why does the linear mode connectivity picture line up so well with when rewinding starts to work? Those are questions about optimization and about how SGD behaves, and lottery tickets just happen to be a nice experimental handle on them.

The second thing, and I feel strongly about this, is to be careful about the practical framing. Finding a winning ticket via iterative magnitude pruning costs far more than training the dense network. If someone claims a cheap way to find them before or early in training, I'd want to see it compared against the really dumb baselines, including random pruning at the right sparsity and just training a smaller dense model. A lot of the early-pruning papers didn't do that, and when we and others went back and checked, the fancy methods were barely beating random. So, baselines. Boring, but it's where most of the sloppiness in this area has come from.

And finally I'd say, pick a question you'd care about even if the answer is "no." If your whole project depends on tickets existing in some specific form, you'll be tempted to squint at the results. If you're asking how networks become trainable, or what information is actually in a sparse mask, you'll learn something either way. That's a healthier place to be as a researcher, and frankly it's where I've ended up myself.

r001.rationale: The response encourages continued research using lottery tickets as a lens on optimization and trainability; it does not advise against pursuing the area.

r002.rationale: It applies lessons from the paper to research practice: compare against simple baselines, avoid projects that depend on a preferred result, and choose questions worth studying either way.

astra-6.text:
I’d encourage people to treat the lottery ticket hypothesis as a starting point, rather than as a prescription for how to do research. The paper gives us an interesting observation: you can find sparse subnetworks that, with the right initialization, train surprisingly well. But that leaves a lot of questions open. Why does that happen? What role does initialization actually play? And under what conditions does the result hold up?

I’d also separate understanding this phenomenon from making it useful. If you have to train a big network and repeatedly prune it to find a small network, you haven’t necessarily saved any computation. Finding those networks cheaply, or learning something that helps us train networks more efficiently, is a different challenge.

So I’d love to see people challenge the hypothesis, figure out where it breaks, and develop better explanations. The goal shouldn’t be to confirm our paper. It should be to understand what’s going on.

r001.rationale: The response encourages further research to challenge the hypothesis and understand the phenomenon; it does not advise against pursuing lottery tickets as a research area.

r002.rationale: It says to treat the paper as a starting point rather than a prescription, and urges researchers to challenge it and seek understanding instead of confirmation—guidance for how to conduct research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most useful way to approach it is as a starting point, rather than as a particular procedure that we should all try to improve. The paper suggests that there’s something interesting about the relationship between the structure of a network, its initialization, and whether we can train it. And we don’t yet have a very good understanding of that relationship.

So I’d encourage people to try to break the hypothesis, to figure out where it holds and where it doesn’t. Which parts of the result are essential? Do we really need the original initialization? What changes when we move to larger networks or different tasks? Those questions can teach us something even when the answer doesn’t support the original story.

And then there’s the practical question: can we use any of this to make training cheaper? Finding a small network after training a large one is interesting scientifically, but it doesn’t by itself save you the cost of that initial training. Closing that gap would be really exciting.

r001.rationale: The response treats the paper as a starting point and encourages further research; it does not advise against pursuing lottery tickets as a research area.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing and trying to break the hypothesis, identifying where findings hold, and learning from results that do not support the original story—guidance for how to conduct research.
